newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan readies death penalty for gun-running.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan readies death penalty for gun-running.

text.p: Pakistan, determined to crack down on ethnic, sectarian and criminal violence, is toughening its laws to make gun-running punishable by death or life imprisonment, an official statement said on Saturday.

It said President Farooq Leghari, on the advice of the new government led by Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, had promulgated an ordinance amending the Pakistan Arms Ordinance 1965 on Friday night. It must be approved by parliament within 120 days.

"Whosoever transports, sells or keeps, offers or exposes for sale a cannon, grenade, rocket launcher, missile, machinegun, sub-machinegun, dynamite or detonator, or ammunition which can be fired from such arms...shall be sentenced to death or imprisonment for life," the amended ordinance says.
It also empowers the government to confiscate the property of an offender and seize any vehicle, vessel, aircraft or any other means of transport used for gun-running.
The punishment for keeping an unlicenced weapon will be increased to a minimum of seven years in prison and a maximum of life imprisonment.
Pakistan has been flooded with weaponry since the 1980s when it served as the main conduit for arming Afghan mujahideen guerrillas fighting Soviet troops in their country.
The semi-autonomous tribal area in North West Frontier Province bordering Afghanistan still does a thriving trade in smuggled weapons ranging from pistols to artillery pieces.
Many of the weapons are in the hands of rival militant Islamic groups, ethnic organisations and criminal gangs.
Ready access to guns and ammunition helped stoke a long struggle between the security forces and the ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM) in Karachi that subsided last year.
This year militant Sunni and Shi'ite Moslem groups have pursued a long-running vendetta with bombs, guns and grenades, particularly in the populous province of Punjab.
Sectarian strife cost at least 170 lives in Pakistan last year and has killed more than 40 people so far this year.
A government spokesman said Sharif's cabinet had decided at its first session on Wednesday and Thursday to toughen the penalties for carrying illegal weapons.
The meetings, which focused on law and order, were attended by provincial governors, chief ministers, chief secretaries and the inspector generals of police of the four provinces.
The spokesman said the changes in the law was an attempt to strike at armed groups without actually banning them.
"It would have been difficult for the government to ban militant organisations, but the effect of the new law will be almost the same," he said.
